# 03 — Classify the research bench and delete what the product already covers

**What to build:** Every script under the research bench gets exactly one verdict — the Rust product already covers it, it is still an instrument, or it cannot work against this build — and the covered and dead ones are deleted rather than described. Instruments are left alone: they are the apparatus tickets 06–10 run on, and rewriting them mid-experiment is the thing to avoid.

**Blocked by:** None — can start immediately

**Status:** ready-for-agent

- [x] Every script has a recorded verdict with a one-line reason.
- [x] Scripts whose capability the Rust product already implements are deleted.
- [x] Scripts that cannot work against this build are deleted.
- [x] Instruments survive untouched, and the list of them is what tickets 06–10 draw from.
- [x] Nothing the product or the remaining experiments depend on is deleted.

## Verdicts

31 Python scripts and one PowerShell script, each with one verdict. Twenty-one files were deleted in
all: eighteen Python scripts, the PowerShell script, and two `.cmd` wrappers. Thirteen Python scripts
survive as instruments.

### Covered by the product — deleted

The capability is now implemented in Rust, and the Rust version is the one that is correct. Every
harvest-family script here tests candidates against segment bytes; the bench's versions all predate
the 752-byte probe alignment fix, so their "0 hits" readings were artefacts of the bug.

| Script | Why it goes |
| --- | --- |
| `scan_ctypes.py` | ReadProcessMemory-only key scan — its own docstring names `evmedia-win/scan.rs` as the target, and that is now what the product does. |
| `fast_scan.py` | Scans memory for 32-hex candidates and tests them against the recently-written segments; that candidate path is `keyscan::recover`. |
| `harvest_all.py` | Memory scan, test against every downloaded segment, write JSON — the same job as `grab` plus `keyscan::recover`. |
| `harvest_keys.py` | Collects every 32-hex string and tries each as a key — superseded by the same path. |
| `scan_keys_all.py` | `harvest_keys.py` with a better target set; superseded the same way. |
| `try_keys.py` | Tests captured keys against real ciphertext — that test is `keyscan::recover`. |
| `ev2_grab.py` | The entire Python pipeline, harvest through merge; the Rust `grab` does all of it, including resume. |
| `drive_playhead.py` | Posts arrow keys to steer the playhead; `evmedia-win::playhead` does this, and its docstring says so. |

### Cannot work against this build — deleted

| Script | Why it goes |
| --- | --- |
| `ev2_batch.py` | Derives keys from manifests with the documented salt formula. That formula does not hold in this build, so without a salt it has no route to a key. |
| `hunt_salt.py` | Searches for the `tk + filename + salt` concatenation in memory. The decisive negative is that this build never builds that string. |
| `compare_tk.py` | Exists only to feed the tk-derivation family, which is the same disproven formula. |
| `find_b64.py` | Locates the base64 decoder by watching alphabet tables; repeated full-memory runs found nothing, and ticket 06 no longer needs the decoder. |
| `aes_map.py` | Static function-boundary mapping of the AES region — needs a disassembler the bench does not have, and the entry points it sought (`0x791F90`, `0x792c78`) are already known. |
| `aes_disasm.py` | Same static route to the same already-known RVA. |
| `disas.py` | Same static route again, against a live module; it times out. |
| `walk_aes.py` | Hooks the AES T-table site and walks up to its caller. The callers live in heap-generated code, so the walk reaches nothing — that is the finding, not a bug in the script. |
| `hexdiff.py` | The differential scan is broken (returns in 0.1 s with zero rows, i.e. it never scanned), and its question is now asked directly by ticket 07's write breakpoint, which needs no diff. |
| `_extract.py` | A one-off that pulled text out of a single, long-superseded session transcript into a log. It is not apparatus for anything pending. |
| `find_segments.ps1` | Its RVAs point at this build's M3U8 parser, not at key derivation. It has failed every time it was run. |

### Wrappers on the dead offline path — deleted

- `一键抓取.cmd` — exists only to run `find_segments.ps1`.
- `解密转MP4.cmd` — consumes the `evplayer2_manifest.json` that `find_segments.ps1` would have produced, so it cannot run either.

The vendored third-party directories and the two `.zip` archives (`EVPlayer2_解密工具与参数/`,
`EVPlayer2通用解密工具/`, and both zips) are **left in place**. They are not bench scripts, they are
tracked, and the zips are the authoritative copy of the vendor material. They sit on the same dead
offline path as the two wrappers above — worth knowing, but removing someone else's artefact is not
this ticket.

### Instruments — kept untouched

These are what tickets 06–10 draw from. `probe_urls.py` and `capture_all.py` overlap (the latter is
the v6 successor to the former); both are kept, because pruning apparatus mid-experiment is the thing
this ticket exists to avoid.

- **Ticket 06 (the API AES as an oracle):** `probe_at.py`, `hook_aes_key.py`, `find_aes_key.py`, `extract_bodies.py`.
- **Ticket 07 (the instruction that writes a segment key):** `probe_at.py`, `probe_schedule_key.py`, `wait_ready.py`, `watch_key.py`.
- **Ticket 08 (the `getDownEVSKey` plaintext):** `capture_all.py`, `sniff_plain.py`, `fish_api_plain.py`, `probe_urls.py`.
- **Both / general:** `hook_caller.py`, `find_in_mem.py`.

### Dependency check

Nothing the product or the remaining experiments need was deleted. A repo-wide search for each
deleted name found only: `HANDOFF.md` (historical narrative, handled in ticket 05), `captured/harvest_all.log`
(capture evidence, which stays), and `scan_keys_all.py` inside the harvest family, deleted with it.
`disas.py`'s only other match is `tools/device_analysis/disasm.py`, a different file in a different
directory, untouched.

# 01 — Merge the two player stand-ins into one, and keep the sweep’s gap handling covered

**What to build:** One seam instead of two. `Harvester` becomes the single stand-in for a live player: it gains `Playhead` as a supertrait and loses its own `seek_to`, so the harvest loop hands the harvester itself to the seek. The sweep’s three existing tests keep every assertion but are re-pointed at that seam — they assert where the playhead arrived, not which index a seek was called with, which is the stronger claim.

**Blocked by:** None — can start immediately

**Status:** ready-for-agent

- [x] `Harvester` extends `Playhead`, and `Harvester::seek_to` no longer exists.
- [x] The harvest fixture implements the window/step pair, and no test implements `seek_to`.
- [x] The three sweep tests still assert: the seek targeted the earliest missing index and the merge afterwards completed; a source that cannot move the playhead is asked once and then left alone; a playhead that answers yes and changes nothing still terminates at the attempt cap.
- [x] The seek tests keep their own minimal playhead — that one is a unit under test, not a second product seam.
- [x] `cargo test --workspace` passes with no new warnings.
- [x] Mutation check: reverting the behaviour each sweep test pins makes that test fail.

The claim the sweep tests make is now about where the playhead *arrived*, which survives any change of
stepping strategy — the old assertion was about which index a seek was asked for, which a rewrite of
the calibration could satisfy while the playhead still went nowhere. `seek_window_to` is generic over

traits on the same object — nothing a test has to stand in for twice.

Turns a running EVPlayer2 into a per-lesson capture: recover the segment keys out of the live player, download the ciphertext, decrypt it, and merge it into a playable MP4. Rust workspace (`evmedia-core` portable, `evmedia-win` the only crate holding Windows APIs, `evmedia` the CLI, `evmedia-gui` a Tauri window whose interactions *are* CLI runs).

## The correction this branch carries

This is the part worth reviewing closely.

A previous round declared that the playback context's `+0x120` key-schedule slot holds no key, and **deleted the code that read it** on that basis. The evidence was a brute-force that returned zero hits every time.

The brute-force was broken. It probed 376 bytes, and the plaintext has to be a whole number of AES blocks for AES to accept it — 376 is 188×2, but 188×2 is not a multiple of 16. The smallest common multiple of 188 and 16 is **752** (188×4). Every probe was rejected, an exception was swallowed, and the result read as "no key here". The conclusion then outlived the bug that produced it: nobody re-ran the experiment after the probe length was fixed.

Measured directly against a live player, `tools/parser-tools/probe_schedule_key.py`: **333 filled slots → 333 keys reconstructed → 333 segments opened, 0 failures.** A later run: **369 of 369.** The first 16 bytes of the schedule are the key's first 16 characters verbatim; the second 16 are MixColumns-transformed, and the derivation inverts it.

So the derivation is back, and it is now the *first* source the loop reads — a live context yields the index, the filename and the key together, with nothing to search for and nothing to test. The heap-wide candidate scan stays for what contexts cannot reach, because a key outlives the context that carried it and afterwards it is only a loose 32-hex string that has to be tested against segment bytes. Neither source covers the other's ground.

`crates/evmedia-core/tests/crypto.rs` pins the real recorded pair so this cannot silently regress again.

## What else is in here

**Segment capture (`evmedia grab`).** Reads the player's live keys, downloads the signed URLs, decrypts (`AES-256-ECB(ciphertext XOR MD5(filename)[:16])`, key = the segment's own 32 hex characters used directly as key bytes), merges by segment index, remuxes with ffmpeg. Resumes from what is already decrypted. One ordering rule is load-bearing and easy to state too strongly: **the download must never be gated on already holding a key** — that is circular, and the version before this one fetched only segments it already had keys for, so a segment whose key had not arrived yet was never downloaded at all.

**Sweep.** A segment's key exists only once the player has decrypted it for playback, so a gap the playhead already ran past can never be filled by waiting. The loop notices the gap and walks the playhead back onto it. Stepping is a `PostMessage` of `WM_KEYDOWN`/`WM_KEYUP` to the player's own window — no focus stealing, no injection, no UI coordinates. Measured at roughly 12 segments/second against 1.35/s real playback.

**One player seam (ticket 01).** `Harvester` has `Playhead` as a supertrait and its own `seek_to` is gone, so the loop hands the harvester itself to `seek_window_to`. The three sweep tests keep every assertion but now state it as *where the playhead arrived* rather than which index a seek was called with.

**Bench classification (ticket 03).** 21 files removed: 18 scripts the Rust product now covers, plus the ones that cannot work against this build (the salt formula does not hold here, the disassembler is absent, the AES callers live in heap-generated code). 13 instruments stay, untouched, for the follow-up work.

**Disk hygiene and redaction (tickets 04, 05).** 1.6 GB of finished-run leavings deleted, all outside version control. `HANDOFF.md` committed with its tokens, signatures and complete request sample replaced by shape-preserving placeholders.

## Tests

`cargo test --workspace` → **45 pass, 0 fail**; `cargo check --all-targets --workspace` warning-free.

Every test added in this branch was mutation-checked — revert the behaviour the test claims to pin, confirm the test fails. For the three sweep tests: making the gap invisible to the loop fails all three, retrying an unbound seek fails the one it pins, removing the attempt cap fails two.

The harvest loop's resume, retry, completeness, sweep and merge behaviour is testable with no player, no Windows and no network, through a fixture that implements the same trait `WinSource` does.

## Is it all done?

No. Directly:

**Working and verified end to end** — key recovery from a live player, download, decrypt, merge, remux, resume, and the sweep mechanism. Two finished videos are on disk; a 79-minute one decodes with zero errors.

**Not done:**

Turns a running EVPlayer2 into a per-lesson capture: recover the segment keys out of the live player, download the ciphertext, decrypt it, and merge it into a playable MP4. Rust workspace (`evmedia-core` portable, `evmedia-win` the only crate holding Windows APIs, `evmedia` the CLI, `evmedia-gui` a Tauri window whose interactions *are* CLI runs).

## The correction this branch carries

This is the part worth reviewing closely.

A previous round declared that the playback context's `+0x120` key-schedule slot holds no key, and **deleted the code that read it** on that basis. The evidence was a brute-force that returned zero hits every time.

The brute-force was broken. It probed 376 bytes, and the plaintext has to be a whole number of AES blocks for AES to accept it — 376 is 188×2, but 188×2 is not a multiple of 16. The smallest common multiple of 188 and 16 is **752** (188×4). Every probe was rejected, an exception was swallowed, and the result read as "no key here". The conclusion then outlived the bug that produced it: nobody re-ran the experiment after the probe length was fixed.

Measured directly against a live player, `tools/parser-tools/probe_schedule_key.py`: **333 filled slots → 333 keys reconstructed → 333 segments opened, 0 failures.** A later run: **369 of 369.** The first 16 bytes of the schedule are the key's first 16 characters verbatim; the second 16 are MixColumns-transformed, and the derivation inverts it.

So the derivation is back, and it is now the *first* source the loop reads — a live context yields the index, the filename and the key together, with nothing to search for and nothing to test. The heap-wide candidate scan stays for what contexts cannot reach, because a key outlives the context that carried it and afterwards it is only a loose 32-hex string that has to be tested against segment bytes. Neither source covers the other's ground.

`crates/evmedia-core/tests/crypto.rs` pins the real recorded pair so this cannot silently regress again.

**Segment capture (`evmedia grab`).** Reads the player's live keys, downloads the signed URLs, decrypts (`AES-256-ECB(ciphertext XOR MD5(filename)[:16])`, key = the segment's own 32 hex characters used directly as key bytes), merges by segment index, remuxes with ffmpeg. Resumes from what is already decrypted. One ordering rule is load-bearing and easy to state too strongly: **the download must never be gated on already holding a key** — that is circular, and the version before this one fetched only segments it already had keys for, so a segment whose key had not arrived yet was never downloaded at all.

**Sweep.** A segment's key exists only once the player has decrypted it for playback, so a gap the playhead already ran past can never be filled by waiting. **Disk hygiene and redaction (tickets 04, 05).** 1.6 GB of finished-run leavings deleted, all outside version control. `HANDOFF.md` committed with its tokens, signatures and complete request sample replaced by shape-preserving placeholders.

## Tests

`cargo test --workspace` → **45 pass, 0 fail**; `cargo check --all-targets --workspace` warning-free.

Every test added in this branch was mutation-checked — revert the behaviour the test claims to pin, confirm the test fails. For the three sweep tests: making the gap invisible to the loop fails all three, retrying an unbound seek fails the one it pins, removing the attempt cap fails two.

The harvest loop's resume, retry, completeness, sweep and merge behaviour is testable with no player, no Windows and no network, through a fixture that implements the same trait `WinSource` does.

## Is it all done?

No. Directly:

**Working and verified end to end** — key recovery from a live player, download, decrypt, merge, remux, resume, and the sweep mechanism. Two finished videos are on disk; a 79-minute one decodes with zero errors.

审查两轴都回来了。这一轮**不是只读的**——变异验证抓出三条测试是假证据，我修好了，另外改正了两处我自己写下的不实声明。

## Standards

**硬性违规：无。** 所有 `.rs` 都在 420 行以内；`evmedia-core` 不含 `windows_sys`；`evmedia-gui` 未链接核心——三项都有测试守着。

有一处要澄清：审查代理把"注释规则"标成了仓库明示标准并据此判了四条硬性违规。我核对后**那条规则不在仓库里**——AGENTS.md 里唯一提到注释的一句是"别改动相邻的注释"，几乎是反的。是我在给代理的提示里把它当成仓库标准写进去了，所以那四条（[capture.rs](crates/evmedia-win/src/capture.rs)、[grab.rs](crates/evmedia-core/src/harvest/grab.rs)、[sweep.rs](crates/evmedia-win/src/sweep.rs)、[seek.rs](crates/evmedia-core/tests/seek.rs) 中叙述改动来源的注释）只能算判断题，不是仓库违规。

**判断题（基线异味）：**

1. **重复代码** — `playhead::press` 与 `WinSource::step` 同形（都是 `player_window` → `post_key`）。
2. **重复代码** — 吸收活密钥的逻辑散在三处：`sweep.rs::absorb_live`、`grab.rs`、`capture.rs`。
3. **重复说明** — "134 个 context 只有 2 个已解密"这段论证在 [seek.rs](crates/evmedia-core/src/harvest/seek.rs) 和 [source.rs](crates/evmedia-win/src/source.rs) 各写了一遍。
4. **原始类型执念** — `KeyEntry.key: String` 让 CONTEXT.md 明确区分的"活密钥形态（32 位十六进制）"与"存储形态（64 位）"共用一个类型。
5. **数据团** — `(u32, (String, String))` 一路同行。
6. **名不副实** — [grab.rs:68](crates/evmedia-core/src/harvest/grab.rs:68) 的 `places: HashMap<String,u32>` 存的是课时序号。
7. **词汇漂移** — CONTEXT.md 写 "Sweep … *Avoid*: seek"，但模块叫 `seek.rs`、函数叫 `seek_window_to`、日志却打 `sweep {round}`。

**两处播放头推进实现**（我上次担心的那条）：代理判定**职责不同，不该合并**，理由站得住——`seek.rs` 是双向、自校准、有目标；`sweep.rs` 是单向、固定批量、无目标，硬合并会给前向遍历套一个它没有的收敛契约。真正该消除的是上面第 1 条。

## Spec

**声明不实（已改）**：US17 原文说 seek 的断言"survive a change of stepping strategy"——不成立，测试同时钉着 `steps()`，换批量就会挂。PR 描述里"本分支每条新增测试都做过变异验证"同样不成立。两处都已改正，并在 spec 和工单里**标注为更正**而不是悄悄替换。

**已完成但文档发霉（已改）**：工单 03 的仪器清单漏了新建的 `probe_write.py`；工单 12 的"工作树无未决文件"在新建脚本后不再成立。

**范围外**：`recover` 子命令与 `keyscan` 不在十二张工单里——那是更早提交的工作，工单是**建在它基础上**切的。属实，但不是这次的越界。

**诚实记录**：工单 12 明确写了"11 未完成仍开 PR"及其理由，没有偷偷绕过阻塞边。

## 这一轮审查改动了代码

变异验证的核心发现：**三条测试是因为别的理由通过的**。

- `a_rerun_resumes_and_reproduces_the_same_bytes` 读 `lesson.ts` 前没删它，第二次读到的是第一次留下的文件；把 `fetch::resume` 换成空表，测试照样过。
- `a_segment_that_cannot_be_decrypted_is_given_up_on_rather_than_retried_forever` 三次空轮后就停在 `idle_limit` 上，根本没碰到它名字里的重试上限。
- `hashing_helpers_agree_with_their_own_definitions` 只验空串，一个忽略参数的 `md5_hex` 也能过。

三条都修好了，并回验确认现在会被变异抓住。第二条需要能看见事件，所以给 `Reporter` 加了 `capturing()`——机器通道原本是只写 stdout，导致"唯一效果是发一个事件"的行为无法观测、也就无法被测试钉住。

共 30 条变异，29 条被抓。唯一没抓住的是 `schedule_to_key` 的堆填充值判断，它**冗余**（填充字节本来也过不了 UTF-8 和十六进制检查），行为另有测试钉住，所以留作意图声明。

另外写了 [probe_write.py](tools/parser-tools/probe_write.py) —— 工单 07 原本要用的仪器跑不了。

**Standards 轴：7 条判断题，0 条硬性违规，最重的是三处重复的活密钥吸收逻辑。Spec 轴：3 条声明/文档问题（全部已改），1 条范围说明。**

全部是这样：**一次坐下，四个实验**。剩下的三张工单是写结论，不需要播放器。

Let me analyse the three results carefully.

**Result 1 & 2: `probe_write.py` — armed but caught nothing.**

Run 1: found 491 contexts, 438 with an empty key field. Picked one, armed the page guard on `0x1ad4fb50000`. Then "done." — **no WRITE reported**.

Run 2: found 938 contexts, 872 empty. Armed on `0x1ad4fb9a000`. Again **no WRITE**.

Critical observations:
1. **The field offset printed is wrong**: `field 0x1ad4fb50600` with `at 0x1ad4fb504e0` being the context. So `field = ctx + 0x120 = 0x1ad4fb504e0 + 0x120 = 0x1ad4fb50600`. ✓ correct.
2. **Page base**: `0x1ad4fb50600 & ~0xfff = 0x1ad4fb50000`. ✓ correct.
3. But the message says `field 0x1ad4fb50600 <heap-code>` — fine.
4. **No write was ever caught in 240 seconds.**

Why? Several hypotheses:

(a) **The guard never fires for target-thread writes** — the concern I flagged as unverified. If `MemoryAccessMonitor` only works... hmm, no, it's a standard mechanism.

(b) **The writer writes to a *different* context than the one I armed on.** I armed on index 0 of 438 empty contexts. The player may have been decrypting a different one.

(c) **The player wasn't actually decoding new segments.** The user ran it twice; between runs the context count doubled (491 → 938), which suggests the player was accumulating contexts (playback moving). But maybe I picked a context that never gets written.

(d) **`MemoryAccessMonitor` on a page that the player accesses very frequently... no, the opposite — no access at all.**

(e) **The `onAccess` callback requires the page to be *touched*; if the writer writes with a large `memcpy`/`rep movs`, the guard fires once at the first byte — but `d.address` would be *before* the field, and my filter `d.address.compare(field) < 0` rejects it!** That's a very plausible bug: a bulk copy or a write starting earlier in the page would be filtered out by my strict `[field, field+32)` window check. And since I `return` without reporting, I'd see nothing.

That's a strong candidate. My filter is too strict: it discards any write to the guarded page that doesn't land exactly in the 32-byte window. But the *first* access to a guarded page after re-arming could be any byte in the page — and frida's MemoryAccessMonitor fires on the *first* access to the page, then... hmm, actually frida disables the guard and re-arms after the callback. So the first write to the page might be to a *different* byte, and my callback returns early — and (depending on frida's re-arm behaviour) that could be fine or could be the only shot.

Hmm. Actually, in frida's MemoryAccessMonitor, the guard is on the *page*; the callback gets the exact address that faulted. After the callback, frida restores the guard. So subsequent accesses will fire again. So a write to another part of the page fires, gets filtered, and the guard is restored. Fine. So eventually a write to my 32 bytes should fire.

Unless... the writes to the field happen via a mechanism that doesn't fault: e.g. the page is **already mapped with the data written by a memcpy from another thread**, or the field is written by a **`rep movs`** where the CPU faults once (on the first byte of the whole copy) and, while the guard is off, the entire copy completes — including my 32 bytes. Then my filter sees `d.address` = the start of the copy (elsewhere in the page, or even a different page!) and discards it.

That last one is very plausible: frida's MemoryAccessMonitor disables the guard, invokes the callback, then re-arms. So during a multi-byte copy, only ONE fault occurs, at the first byte touched. If the field is written by a 32-byte or larger copy starting before `field`, the only callback has `d.address < field` → my filter rejects it and I learn nothing.

**So my filter is the bug.** I should not filter so strictly — or rather, I should *report* every write to the page (with the address) rather than silently dropping ones outside the window. That's the fix.

Hmm, but careful about the 24-hit cap... I have no cap. If I report every write to the page I might flood. But it's ONE page; and the player's access to that page is probably rare.

Also: another very plausible hypothesis — **the field at +0x120 is written as part of writing the whole context object**, i.e. by a bulk copy of the object (e.g. `memcpy(dst, src, 0x2a8)`). Then the fault is at the object's start, not the field.

So the fix: in `onAccess`, report EVERY write to the guarded page with its address and offset relative to the context, and don't pre-filter. Then a human/next run can see which write covers the field.

Hmm, and also: I should guard the page containing the *context start*, or better, report the range. Actually simplest: report the first N writes to the page with `d.address`, `d.from`, and the delta from `field`.

Also: (f) another hypothesis — **the player simply wasn't decrypting new segments during those 240 s.** Both runs printed "done." with no write at all. Note run 1 found 438 empty contexts and run 2 found 872 empty — so the player was *adding* contexts. But were they being decrypted? The readiness flag `ready` is at +0x264; 872 still empty means they weren't decrypted. Hmm — so the player was loading contexts without decrypting them. That could mean the lesson was paused, or the player pre-loads contexts.

Hmm, important: is `ready` at +0x264 even the right flag? I took it from `watch_key.py`: `ready: obj.add(0x264).readU8()`. And HANDOFF says `+0x268` is the mask, `+0x120` the schedule. And probe_schedule_key.py found "333 filled slots". So the empty-check via `0xBAADF00D` at +0x120 is the reliable signal — 438 contexts have fill, i.e. no key.

So the player had 438 undecrypted contexts and never decrypted one in 240 s? Plausible if playback was paused or the user was browsing.

But the user said they'd open a lesson. Hmm.

**Result 3: `probe_at.py` on 0x792c78.** One hit. Very informative:
- Stack contains `0|0|119354-4d91b321-....ts` — the `<type>|<idx>|<filename>` form HANDOFF mentioned.
- Stack contains the full signed URL `http://cn28027.evplayer.cn/b83a7c8f-.../119354-4d91b321-...ts`
- Stack contains `"-a257-50ecf8c38d88/119354-4d91b321-....ts' for reading"` — that's an error message fragment! "'<path>' for reading" is the tail of a file-open error like `cannot open '<path>' for reading` or `Failed to open '<path>' for reading`.
- Stack contains `uthorization` (Authorization header).

    print('   the target did %d reads of the page before writing' % reads)
    return 0 if saw_write else 1


if __name__ == '__main__':
    sys.exit(main())

SRC = r"C:\Users\Yonjay\AppData\Local\Temp\watchprobe\src\main.rs"
EXE = r"C:\Users\Yonjay\AppData\Local\Temp\watchprobe\relay.exe"

STUB_OLD = """try {
  if (chooseTargets()) arm();
} catch (e) {
  send({t: 'err', where: 'setup', e: String(e)});
}"""


def extract_js():
    src = open(TOOL, encoding='utf-8').read()
    js = src.split('JS = r"""', 1)[1].split('"""', 1)[0]
    assert STUB_OLD in js, 'the setup block moved; update this harness'
    return js


def build():
    r = subprocess.run(['rustc', '-O', '-o', EXE, SRC], capture_output=True, text=True,
                       encoding='utf-8', errors='replace')
    if r.returncode != 0:
        print(r.stderr[-2000:])
        sys.exit(1)


def main():
    build()
    js = extract_js()

    p = subprocess.Popen([EXE], stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
                         text=True, encoding='utf-8', errors='replace', bufsize=1)
    lines = []
    threading.Thread(target=lambda: [lines.append(l.rstrip()) for l in p.stdout],
                     daemon=True).start()
    for _ in range(200):
        if len(lines) >= 3:
            break
        time.sleep(0.02)
    pid = int(lines[0].split('=')[1])
    base = lines[1].split('=')[1]
    page = hex(int(base, 16) & ~0xFFF)
    print('target pid=%d base=%s page=%s\n' % (pid, base, page))

    stub = ("var watched = [{ page: '%s', fieldOff: 0x120, file: 'TEST.ts', index: 7, ctx: '%s' }];\n"
            "var ranges = [{ base: ptr('%s'), size: 0x1000 }];\n"
            "arm();" % (page, base, page))
    js = js.replace(STUB_OLD, stub)

    session = frida.attach(pid)
    script = session.create_script(js)
    out = []
    script.on('message', lambda m, d: out.append(m))
    script.load()
    time.sleep(6.0)
    session.detach()
    p.kill()

    print('=== the tool said ===')
    saw_write = False
    saw_writer = False
    for m in out:
        pl = m.get('payload') or {}
        t = pl.get('t')
        if t == 'access':
            print('   [access] %-5s page+%-6s from %s%s'
                  % (pl['op'], pl['off'], pl['from'],
                     '   <<< lands on a key field' if pl.get('field') else ''))
        elif t == 'write':
            saw_write = True
            print('   *** WRITE into a key field: instruction=%s file=%s value=%r'
                  % (pl['by'], pl['file'], pl['value']))
        elif t == 'writer':
            saw_writer = True
            print('   *** writer context: at=%s regs=%s' % (pl['at'], pl.get('regs')))
            print('       stack: %s' % (pl.get('stack') or [])[:6])
            print('       backtrace: %s' % (pl.get('bt') or [])[:4])
        elif t == 'log':
            print('   [*] %s' % pl['msg'])
        elif t == 'err':
            print('   [err] %s: %s' % (pl.get('where'), pl.get('e')))
        elif m.get('type') == 'error':
            print('   [script error] %s' % str(m.get('description'))[:300])

    print()
    print('=== did it survive the reads and catch the write? ===')
    print('   write caught  :', saw_write)
    print('   writer dumped :', saw_writer)
    reads = len([l for l in lines if l.startswith('read ')])
    print('   the target did %d reads of the page before writing' % reads)
    return 0 if saw_write else 1


if __name__ == '__main__':
    sys.exit(main())

"""Run probe_write.py's real watch machinery against a stand-in target.

The synthetic target reads the guarded page several times before writing the 'key' into the watched
field -- the exact sequence that silenced the first version of the script. chooseTargets() is stubbed
out because it needs the player's DLL; everything else (onAccess, the field match, the timer re-arm,
the catch handling) is the shipped code, unmodified.
"""
import re
import subprocess
import sys
import threading
import time

import frida

TOOL = r"D:\Codes\github\ev-reverse\tools\parser-tools\probe_write.py"
SRC = r"C:\Users\Yonjay\AppData\Local\Temp\watchprobe\src\main.rs"
EXE = r"C:\Users\Yonjay\AppData\Local\Temp\watchprobe\relay.exe"

STUB_OLD = """try {
  if (chooseTargets()) arm();
} catch (e) {
  send({t: 'err', where: 'setup', e: String(e)});
}"""


def extract_js():
    src = open(TOOL, encoding='utf-8').read()
    js = src.split('JS = r"""', 1)[1].split('"""', 1)[0]
    assert STUB_OLD in js, 'the setup block moved; update this harness'
    return js


def build():
    r = subprocess.run(['rustc', '-O', '-o', EXE, SRC], capture_output=True, text=True,
                       encoding='utf-8', errors='replace')
    if r.returncode != 0:
        print(r.stderr[-2000:])
        sys.exit(1)


def main():
    build()
    js = extract_js()

    p = subprocess.Popen([EXE], stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
                         text=True, encoding='utf-8', errors='replace', bufsize=1)
    lines = []
    threading.Thread(target=lambda: [lines.append(l.rstrip()) for l in p.stdout],
                     daemon=True).start()
    for _ in range(200):
        if len(lines) >= 3:
            break
        time.sleep(0.02)
    pid = int(lines[0].split('=')[1])
    base = lines[1].split('=')[1]
    page = hex(int(base, 16) & ~0xFFF)
    print('target pid=%d base=%s page=%s\n' % (pid, base, page))

    stub = ("var watched = [{ page: '%s', fieldOff: 0x120, file: 'TEST.ts', index: 7, ctx: '%s' }];\n"
            "var ranges = [{ base: ptr('%s'), size: 0x1000 }];\n"
            "arm();" % (page, base, page))
    # The DLL lookup also throws in a stand-in process; chooseTargets (stubbed) is its only user.
    js = js.replace("var dll = Process.getModuleByName(DLL);",
                    "var dll = { base: ptr('0x1000') };  // stubbed for this harness")
    js = js.replace(STUB_OLD, stub)

    session = frida.attach(pid)
    script = session.create_script(js)
    out = []
    script.on('message', lambda m, d: out.append(m))
    script.load()
    time.sleep(6.0)
    session.detach()
    p.kill()

    print('=== the tool said ===')
    saw_write = False
    saw_writer = False
    for m in out:
        pl = m.get('payload') or {}
        t = pl.get('t')
        if t == 'access':
            print('   [access] %-5s page+%-6s from %s%s'
                  % (pl['op'], pl['off'], pl['from'],
                     '   <<< lands on a key field' if pl.get('field') else ''))
        elif t == 'write':
            saw_write = True
            print('   *** WRITE into a key field: instruction=%s file=%s (index %s)'
                  % (pl['by'], pl['file'], pl['index']))
        elif t == 'writer':
            saw_writer = True
            print('   *** writer context: at=%s regs=%s' % (pl['at'], pl.get('regs')))
            print('       stack: %s' % (pl.get('stack') or [])[:6])
            print('       backtrace: %s' % (pl.get('bt') or [])[:4])
        elif t == 'value':
            print('   value after the store: %r' % pl['value'])
        elif t == 'log':
            print('   [*] %s' % pl['msg'])
        elif t == 'err':
            print('   [err] %s: %s' % (pl.get('where'), pl.get('e')))
        elif m.get('type') == 'error':
            print('   [script error] %s' % str(m.get('description'))[:300])
            st = m.get('stack')
            if st:
                print('      %s' % str(st)[:400])

    print()
    print('=== did it survive the reads and catch the write? ===')
    print('   write caught  :', saw_write)
    print('   writer dumped :', saw_writer)
    reads = len([l for l in lines if l.startswith('read ')])
    print('   the target did %d reads of the page before writing' % reads)
    return 0 if saw_write else 1


if __name__ == '__main__':
    sys.exit(main())

  6. **A guard faults BEFORE the store executes.** The callback runs, and only when it returns does
     the instruction retry and complete, so reading the field inside the callback always returns the
     old contents. The value is therefore read on a later turn, and the first version's attempt to
     report it inline would have reported zeros.

# 07 — Catch the instruction that writes a segment key into a playback context

**What to build:** A hardware write breakpoint on one empty *schedule*, caught the moment the player fills it. What comes out is the writing instruction and its backtrace — the trail to the derivation. If it cannot be caught, the reason is named rather than left open: a per-thread breakpoint across sixteen threads may simply miss the writer, and that is a result too.

**Blocked by:** None — can start immediately

**Status:** ready-for-human

- [ ] An empty schedule is found and a write breakpoint is armed on it, or the reason no empty one exists is stated.
- [ ] A write is caught, with the instruction pointer and a backtrace — or a named reason it was not caught.
- [ ] The command used and its output are recorded as the evidence.
- [ ] The player is left running, or is restarted and the already-recovered keys are confirmed intact.

## Progress: the first attempt ran, caught nothing, and the cause is now known

Two runs of the first version of `probe_write.py` armed successfully and reported no write at all:

```
found 491 context(s), 438 with an empty key field
empty context: 119354-5c18a0bd-40a8-4402-bf21-15d17e38cb87.ts at 0x1ad4fb504e0 (ready=0)
armed on 0x1ad4fb50000 (... field 0x1ad4fb50600)
done.                                  <- nothing in between, 240 seconds
```

A second run found 938 contexts with 872 empty, armed, and again reported nothing.

The guard had fired. Frida's `MemoryAccessMonitor` works with `PAGE_GUARD`, and **the guard is consumed
by the first access — read or write — and is not restored.** The player reads these context objects
constantly. The first read of the guarded page hit the callback, the callback saw
`d.operation !== 'write'` and returned, and the page was unguarded from that moment on. The run was
blind for the remaining 240 seconds. It was never "the player did not write"; it was "nothing was
reported".

The first version also guarded an arbitrary empty context, chosen by scan order, which is very likely
one the player will never touch again.

## What was measured, and how

The mechanism was then tested against stand-in target processes written for the purpose, because
guessing about `PAGE_GUARD` semantics is what produced the silent failure in the first place.

| Question | Measurement |
| --- | --- |
| Does a target-thread write reach the callback at all? | Yes. A stand-in process's own stores reported normally. |
| How often does the callback fire? | Once. 27 target memory operations produced 1 report. The guard is consumed and not restored. |
| Is re-arming from inside the callback safe? | **No.** 200 reports and the target performed *zero* operations for 8 seconds — it wedged. |
| Is re-arming from a timer cheap? | Yes. A target hammering guarded pages kept 100.4% of its unguarded throughput at 64 and 128 pages, 100 ms re-arm. |
| Is a page guard free of a *store* of a different width? | The reported address is the **faulting byte**, not the write's first byte. A 32-byte store at page+0x120 reported as page+0x130. |
| Is there a hardware watchpoint to fall back on? | **No.** `typeof Thread.setHardwareWatchpoint` and `...Breakpoint` are both `undefined` on frida 17.18.0; `Thread` exposes only `backtrace`. |
| Does a guard fault before or after the store runs? | **Before.** Reading the field inside the callback returns the old contents; the value has to be read on a later turn. |
| Does `Thread.backtrace(..., ACCURATE)` work? | It raises `invalid operation` where unwind data is unusable, and did on a plain Rust target. FUZZY returned an empty list there. |
| `NativePointer.toNumber()` | Does not exist — only `UInt64` has it. Calling it inside the callback raised once per access. |

**This also corrects what the bench believed about `watch_key.py`.** It is not the 96 pages that hang
the player; 128 guarded pages measured free. It hangs because it *also* hooks the AES site and takes an
`ACCURATE` backtrace on every hit, and that site fires once per AES round. The ticket's own fallback —
"a per-thread breakpoint across sixteen threads may simply miss the writer" — describes a mechanism
this frida build does not have at all.

## The instrument now

`tools/parser-tools/probe_write.py` was rewritten around those measurements: it aims at the contexts
just past the highest decrypted index (the ones about to be filled, rather than an arbitrary one),
guards up to 24 pages, re-arms from a 100 ms timer and never from inside the callback, reports every
access with the offset it faulted at, reads the value after the store has completed, and prints a
call chain assembled from module pointers found on the stack when the unwind-based backtrace comes back
empty.

It was run end to end against a stand-in target: six reads of the guarded page (the exact sequence that
silenced the first version), then a 32-byte store into the watched field. It survived the reads, caught
the store, named the instruction, dumped the registers, read `3df51fd02753d5605cc3139e66a3561e` back
correctly, and produced a call chain after both backtracers returned nothing.

**It still has not been run against EVPlayer2 itself.** The stand-in proves the mechanism; only the real
player can answer this ticket.

### How to run it

```
C:\Users\Yonjay\.conda\envs\subgen\python.exe -u tools\parser-tools\probe_write.py 300
```

Preconditions, all load-bearing:

- EVPlayer2 running, logged in through `tools\device_launcher\run-evplayer.cmd`.
- A lesson open **that still has segments the player has not decrypted on this machine.** The writer
  only runs while the player is decrypting something for the first time. Open a lesson never opened
  here, and start the script *before* the segment is reached.
- Keep it playing. Do not pause.

The PATH `python` is a Microsoft Store placeholder and does not work; use the conda path above.

**Success** is `WRITE into a key field` naming the instruction, followed by `the writer, with context`.
**A named negative is also a result** for this ticket, and both likely ones now have a diagnosis:

- `no context with an empty key field` — every context on this machine has been decrypted, so there is
  no store left to catch. The remedy is a lesson that has not been played here.
- `still watching N page(s); 0 access(es) seen so far` repeating — the guarded pages are genuinely not
  being touched, which would mean the contexts chosen are not the ones being decrypted. Say so, and say
  which indexes were being watched.

# 07 — Catch the instruction that writes a segment key into a playback context

**What to build:** A hardware write breakpoint on one empty *schedule*, caught the moment the player fills it. What comes out is the writing instruction and its backtrace — the trail to the derivation. If it cannot be caught, the reason is named rather than left open: a per-thread breakpoint across sixteen threads may simply miss the writer, and that is a result too.

**Blocked by:** None — can start immediately

**Status:** ready-for-human

- [ ] An empty schedule is found and a write breakpoint is armed on it, or the reason no empty one exists is stated.
- [ ] A write is caught, with the instruction pointer and a backtrace — or a named reason it was not caught.
- [ ] The command used and its output are recorded as the evidence.
- [ ] The player is left running, or is restarted and the already-recovered keys are confirmed intact.

## The instrument had to be replaced before this ticket could be run

Found while preparing the human session, and fixed here so the session is not spent on a script that
cannot work.

**`watch_key.py` was the only surviving instrument that could arm a memory write watch, and it is the
one the bench marks "do not run this directly"** — it watches up to 96 pages, re-arms the monitor every
1.2 s, and attaches an `Interceptor` from inside the access callback. On a live player that is enough
to hang it. Handing this ticket that script would have cost the session it exists for.

**The ticket's own fallback is not available either.** It names "a per-thread breakpoint across
sixteen threads" as the thing that might miss the writer. Frida 17.18.0 has no hardware watchpoints:
`typeof Thread.setHardwareWatchpoint` is `undefined`, checked by loading a probe script against a live
process. `MemoryAccessMonitor` — page guards — is the only mechanism that exists on this build, so the
miss to worry about is a guard-page one, not a hardware-slot one.

**So this ticket now runs on a new, deliberately light instrument:** `tools/parser-tools/probe_write.py`.
It finds the playback contexts, picks **one** whose key field still holds the heap fill (`0xBAADF00D`
at `+0x120`, i.e. not yet decrypted), guards that single page, reports the first write to the field,
and disables the monitor immediately — one page, no re-arm loop, no `Interceptor` inside the callback.
The instruction it names is then hooked once, after the fact, to dump registers, stack strings and a
backtrace the next time that instruction runs.

The script is syntax-checked (the JS loads cleanly; the only error is the expected missing-DLL one in a
throwaway process). **It has not been run against the player** — that is what this ticket's session is
for. It is a small script precisely so that it can be corrected live if the mechanism behaves
differently than expected.

### How to run it

```
C:\Users\Yonjay\.conda\envs\subgen\python.exe -u tools\parser-tools\probe_write.py 240
```

"""Find the instruction that fills a playback context's key field, statically.

The context's AES key lives at +0x120. Two consumers are already known:
  hls_decode   @ RVA 0x40af0  (cmp [rcx+0x264],0 ; add rcx,0x120 ; call 0x20ec0)
  a small fn   @ RVA 0x3f4c0  (cmp [rcx+0x264],0 ; add rcx,0x120 ; call 0x20e8c)

The writer has not been found by scanning for stores to [reg+0x120]: the only two such SSE stores
are bulk self-copies. So this looks from the other end -- the OpenSSL key-schedule entry points.
A schedule that decodes back to the key IS an AES key schedule, so whatever derives the key very
likely calls one of them. Among those callers, the writer should be the one that touches +0x120.
"""
import collections
import struct
import sys

import capstone
import pefile

DLL = r"D:\Learning\EVPlayer2\PlayerLibRender56_vs.dll"
pe = pefile.PE(DLL, fast_load=True)
TEXT = next(s for s in pe.sections if s.Name.rstrip(b'\0') == b'.text')
TEXT_VA = TEXT.VirtualAddress
TEXT_DATA = TEXT.get_data()
BASE = pe.OPTIONAL_HEADER.ImageBase
print('image base 0x%x  .text va 0x%x  size 0x%x' % (BASE, TEXT_VA, len(TEXT_DATA)))

PD = next(s for s in pe.sections if s.Name.rstrip(b'\0') == b'.pdata')
FUNCS = []
pdoff = 0
pd = PD.get_data()
while pdoff + 12 <= len(pd):
    s, e, u = struct.unpack_from('<III', pd, pdoff)
    if s:
        FUNCS.append((s, e, u))
    pdoff += 12
FUNCS.sort()
print('pdata functions:', len(FUNCS))
starts = {s for s, _, _ in FUNCS}


def func_of(rva):
    import bisect
    i = bisect.bisect_right([f[0] for f in FUNCS], rva) - 1
    if i >= 0 and FUNCS[i][0] <= rva < FUNCS[i][1]:
        return FUNCS[i]
    return None


md = capstone.Cs(capstone.CS_ARCH_X86, capstone.CS_MODE_64)
md.detail = True

INTEREST = {0x791f90: 'AES_set_encrypt_key', 0x791d10: 'AES_set_decrypt_key',
            0x20ec0: 'app AES init (hls_decode uses)', 0x20e8c: 'app AES init (2nd site uses)'}

# Pass 1: who calls any of the interesting entries?
callers = collections.defaultdict(set)
calls = []
for ins in md.disasm(TEXT_DATA, TEXT_VA):
    if ins.mnemonic == 'call' and ins.operands and ins.operands[0].type == capstone.x86.X86_OP_IMM:
        tgt = ins.operands[0].imm - BASE
        if tgt in INTEREST:
            f = func_of(ins.address - TEXT_VA + TEXT_VA) or func_of(ins.address - TEXT_VA)
            fr = func_of(ins.address - TEXT_VA)
            callers[tgt].add(fr)
            calls.append((tgt, ins.address - TEXT_VA, fr))

for tgt, name in INTEREST.items():
    fs = sorted({f for f in callers.get(tgt, []) if f})
    print('\n%-28s (0x%x): %d caller(s) in %d function(s)' % (name, tgt, len([c for c in calls if c[0]==tgt]), len(fs)))
    for f in fs:
        print('    func [0x%x, 0x%x)' % (f[0], f[1]))

# Pass 2: among those caller functions, which touch +0x120?
print('\n=== among the callers, who touches [reg+0x120]? ===')
candidate_funcs = sorted({f for fs in callers.values() for f in fs if f})
for f in candidate_funcs:
    s, e, _ = f
    off = s - TEXT_VA
    n = e - s
    if off < 0 or off + n > len(TEXT_DATA):
        continue
    hits = []
    for ins in md.disasm(TEXT_DATA[off:off + n], s):
        for op in ins.operands:
            if op.type == capstone.x86.X86_OP_MEM and op.mem.disp == 0x120:
                hits.append((ins.address, ins.mnemonic, ins.op_str))
    if hits:
        print('  func [0x%x, 0x%x):' % (s, e))
        for a, m, o in hits:
            print('      0x%06x  %s %s' % (a, m, o))

unwind)`. A function's entry is a lookup, not a scan. The same is true of `.text` in general — this
DLL is fully statically analysable from the file.

# 06 — Read the API’s AES out of the player with an RPC oracle

**What to build:** The player’s own AES, callable from outside the process. A captured request body decrypts through it, and it accepts any buffer rather than one hard-coded message. The key is never recovered and never needs to be: the point is to stop needing it.

**Blocked by:** None — can start immediately

**Status:** ready-for-human

- [ ] A buffer can be handed to the player’s AES and the transformed buffer comes back.
- [ ] A captured request body decrypts to readable plaintext through it.
- [ ] The oracle accepts an arbitrary input, not one captured message.
- [ ] The command used and its output are recorded as the evidence.

## What is already in place, and the one gap

Written up while preparing the human session, because the second half of this ticket turns out not to
be a script that exists.

**Startable with a surviving instrument.** `probe_at.py` hooks one RVA in a live module and dumps, at
each hit, the registers that point at printable strings, the strings on the stack, and a 32-hex scan.
Run against the AES body it is how the calling convention gets read off:

```
C:\Users\Yonjay\.conda\envs\subgen\python.exe -u tools\parser-tools\probe_at.py PlayerLibRender56_vs.dll 0x792c78 30 0x2000
```

Preconditions: EVPlayer2 running and logged in, then browse the catalogue or open a lesson so the API
call happens while the hook is armed. (`0x792c78` is the instruction that reads the inverse S-box.)
What to read out of the hits: which register holds the input buffer, which holds the output, and
whether a third argument points at an `AES_KEY`. That is what a callable oracle needs.

**The gap: no surviving instrument calls into a module.** The three scripts that use `rpc.exports` —
`find_in_mem.py`, `sniff_plain.py`, `wait_ready.py` — all export memory *scanners*, not calls. So the
oracle itself is a script that has to be written, and it cannot be written honestly until the
calling convention above is known.

**A second gap, inherited from ticket 03.** `0x792c78` is an instruction in the middle of the routine,
not its entry point, and the entry for the *encrypt/decrypt* half has never been confirmed — only
`0x791F90` is known, which is `AES_set_encrypt_key` (OpenSSL signature, and `hook_aes_key.py` caught
2825 keys there, so it is a real entry). To call the AES you need the enclosing entry of `0x792c78`.
Two scripts that were hunting exactly that — `aes_disasm.py` and `aes_map.py` — were deleted by ticket
03, correctly: they needed a disassembler this machine does not have and could not run. Their approach
is recoverable without one, at runtime: scan backwards from `0x792c78` for the nearest compiler
alignment padding (`cc cc cc`) or prologue, and take the address after it. That is a small addition to
the probe, not a new investigation, and it should be done in the same sitting.

## Why this ticket matters more than its size suggests

This is one of the two routes to the thing the project actually wants. If the player's AES can be
called, then `POST /student/getPlayTimeKeySignEVS*` can be replayed from outside for any lesson in the
catalogue, and the segment manifests can be pulled without a human opening anything. That is the
"no play-this-one-fetch-this-one" goal, minus the per-lesson playback that blocks it today.

"no play-this-one-fetch-this-one" goal, minus the per-lesson playback that blocks it today.

## The oracle's entry points, located statically

Found by disassembling the DLL from the file — no player needed for this part. All RVAs, image base
`0x180000000`.

**`0x20EC0` — the app's AES key setup.** `(rcx = the AES_KEY to fill, rdx = ?, r8d = bits, r9d = mode)`.
It selects a block function by mode and stores it, then expands the key:

```
0x020ef0  mov   rdi, rcx
0x020ef3  mov   [rsp+0x28], r9d        ; mode
0x020ef8  mov   ebx, r8d               ; bits
0x020f00  sar   ebx, 5                 ; nk = bits / 32
0x020f03  lea   rax, [rip-0x63a]       ; encrypt block function
0x020f12  lea   rcx, [rip-0xbd9]       ; decrypt block function
0x020f1c  cmovne rax, rcx              ; mode != 0 -> decrypt
0x020f27  mov   [rdi+0x118], rax       ; the chosen block function
0x020f2e  lea   r12d, [rbx+6]          ; rounds = nk + 6
```

The loop that follows (`0x11b`, a `0..0xff` byte table) is the GF(2^8) inverse table — a
constant-time AES, not OpenSSL's T-table version.

**`0x20EA0` — the block-call trampoline.** Call it with `rcx = ctx`:

```
0x020ea0  mov   eax, [rcx+0x110]       ; the round count
0x020ea6  mov   [rsp+0x30], eax
0x020eaa  jmp   qword [rcx+0x118]      ; tail-call the block function
```

So the minimum oracle is two calls and one allocation: allocate ~0x200 bytes for the AES_KEY, call
`0x20EC0` with the key you want to use (mode 0 to encrypt, nonzero to decrypt), then call `0x20EA0`
with that buffer. Nothing has to be recovered from the process, and nothing is hard-coded to one
captured message — which is what the acceptance criteria ask for.

**`AES_set_encrypt_key` at `0x791F90` and `AES_set_decrypt_key` at `0x791D10`** are the OpenSSL T-table
versions, called from 8 and 4 functions respectively, and they are on the *segment* path rather than
this one. `AES_set_encrypt_key` even appears among its own callers, which is the OpenSSL structure
(the decrypt-key routine calls the encrypt-key one).

**`0x3F4C0` — the second consumer of a context's key field.**

```
0x3f4c0  sub   rsp, 0x38
0x3f4c4  cmp   byte [rcx+0x264], 0      ; the ready byte
0x3f4cb  je    +0x1d
0x3f4cd  add   rcx, 0x120               ; the key field
0x3f4d4  mov   dword [rsp+0x28], 1      ; mode = decrypt
0x3f4dc  mov   dword [rsp+0x20], 0
0x3f4dd  call  0x20E98                  ; -> the trampoline above
```

Called from `0x392A4`. With `hls_decode`, that makes **two and only two** places in the whole `.text`
that use `add rcx,0x120` — the segment-key field has exactly two consumers, and both pass it to the
app's AES. That is worth knowing for ticket 09: the field really is an AES key, and the AES is this one.

**A note on what `+0x120` is.** `hls_decode` passes `ctx+0x120` as the *first* argument to the key
setup, i.e. as the AES_KEY to be filled in place. So the 32 bytes this project has been calling "the
schedule" are the head of an expanded key schedule, which is consistent with the empirical relation
`schedule_to_key` inverts — but it means the field is written **by the AES setup**, expanded from a
key handed to it. Whatever produces that input key is ticket 07's writer, and it is one call away
rather than in the same instruction.

# 06 — Read the API’s AES out of the player with an RPC oracle

**What to build:** The player’s own AES, callable from outside the process. A captured request body decrypts through it, and it accepts any buffer rather than one hard-coded message. The key is never recovered and never needs to be: the point is to stop needing it.

**Blocked by:** None — can start immediately

**Status:** ready-for-human

- [ ] A buffer can be handed to the player’s AES and the transformed buffer comes back.
- [ ] A captured request body decrypts to readable plaintext through it.
- [ ] The oracle accepts an arbitrary input, not one captured message.
- [ ] The command used and its output are recorded as the evidence.

## What is already in place, and the one gap

Written up while preparing the human session, because the second half of this ticket turns out not to
be a script that exists.

**Startable with a surviving instrument.** `probe_at.py` hooks one RVA in a live module and dumps, at
each hit, the registers that point at printable strings, the strings on the stack, and a 32-hex scan.
Run against the AES body it is how the calling convention gets read off:

```
C:\Users\Yonjay\.conda\envs\subgen\python.exe -u tools\parser-tools\probe_at.py PlayerLibRender56_vs.dll 0x792c78 30 0x2000
```

Preconditions: EVPlayer2 running and logged in, then browse the catalogue or open a lesson so the API
call happens while the hook is armed. (`0x792c78` is the instruction that reads the inverse S-box.)
What to read out of the hits: which register holds the input buffer, which holds the output, and
whether a third argument points at an `AES_KEY`. That is what a callable oracle needs.

**The gap: no surviving instrument calls into a module.** The three scripts that use `rpc.exports` —
`find_in_mem.py`, `sniff_plain.py`, `wait_ready.py` — all export memory *scanners*, not calls. So the
oracle itself is a script that has to be written, and it cannot be written honestly until the
calling convention above is known.

**A second gap, inherited from ticket 03 — and the recipe written here for it was wrong.** The first
version of this ticket said: "scan backwards from `0x792c78` for the nearest compiler alignment padding
(`cc cc cc`) and take the address after it". Checked against the DLL on disk, that recipe returns the
**wrong function**:

- The bytes at RVA `0x792c78` are `33 6e f8 33 68 0c` = `xor ebp,[rsi-8]; xor ebp,[rax+0xc]` — a
  round-key XOR, **not** the inverse-S-box read this project has been describing. (The S-box reads are
  at `0x792c59` and nearby.)
- `.pdata` says the enclosing function is **`[0x792b1c, 0x792ec3)`**.
- There are **no `cc cc cc` runs at all in `[0x792000, 0x792c78)`**. The nearest one is at `0x791f8d`,
  which is the entry of `AES_set_encrypt_key` — a *different* function. The recipe would have returned
  that one.

**The reliable way is `.pdata`, and the DLL has it.** `PlayerLibRender56_vs.dll` is not packed: six
normal sections, `.pdata` at RVA `0x12a8000` with **19,488** function entries, each `(start, end,
unwind)`. A function's entry is a lookup, not a scan. The same is true of `.text` in general — this
DLL is fully statically analysable from the file.

**And the disassembler this project believed it did not have is installed.** `capstone 5.0.7` and
`pefile 2024.8.26` are both present in `C:\Users\Yonjay\.conda\envs\subgen`. The old note "静态分析不可用：
无 capstone/pefile/dumpbin" is wrong — most likely it was run against the PATH `python`, which is the
Microsoft Store placeholder and has neither. Two scripts were deleted by ticket 03 on that false
premise; see the correction recorded there.

One practical note for anyone writing a disassembly loop: `capstone.Cs.disasm` **stops at the first
undecodable byte** and silently returns a short iteration. Over this DLL it yielded 448 `call`
instructions instead of tens of thousands until `md.skipdata = True` was set. A scan that "found
nothing" is more likely to have stopped early than to have proved an absence.

# 06 — Read the API’s AES out of the player with an RPC oracle

**What to build:** The player’s own AES, callable from outside the process. A captured request body decrypts through it, and it accepts any buffer rather than one hard-coded message. The key is never recovered and never needs to be: the point is to stop needing it.

**Blocked by:** None — can start immediately

**Status:** ready-for-human

- [ ] A buffer can be handed to the player’s AES and the transformed buffer comes back.
- [ ] A captured request body decrypts to readable plaintext through it.
- [ ] The oracle accepts an arbitrary input, not one captured message.
- [ ] The command used and its output are recorded as the evidence.

## What is already in place, and the one gap

Written up while preparing the human session, because the second half of this ticket turns out not to
be a script that exists.

**Startable with a surviving instrument.** `probe_at.py` hooks one RVA in a live module and dumps, at
each hit, the registers that point at printable strings, the strings on the stack, and a 32-hex scan.
Run against the AES body it is how the calling convention gets read off:

```
C:\Users\Yonjay\.conda\envs\subgen\python.exe -u tools\parser-tools\probe_at.py PlayerLibRender56_vs.dll 0x792c78 30 0x2000
```

Preconditions: EVPlayer2 running and logged in, then browse the catalogue or open a lesson so the API
call happens while the hook is armed. (`0x792c78` is the instruction that reads the inverse S-box.)
What to read out of the hits: which register holds the input buffer, which holds the output, and
whether a third argument points at an `AES_KEY`. That is what a callable oracle needs.

**The gap: no surviving instrument calls into a module.** The three scripts that use `rpc.exports` —
`find_in_mem.py`, `sniff_plain.py`, `wait_ready.py` — all export memory *scanners*, not calls. So the
oracle itself is a script that has to be written, and it cannot be written honestly until the
calling convention above is known.

**A second gap, inherited from ticket 03 — and the recipe written here for it was wrong.** The first
version of this ticket said: "scan backwards from `0x792c78` for the nearest compiler alignment padding
(`cc cc cc`) and take the address after it". Checked against the DLL on disk, that recipe returns the
**wrong function**:

- The bytes at RVA `0x792c78` are `33 6e f8 33 68 0c` = `xor ebp,[rsi-8]; xor ebp,[rax+0xc]` — a
  round-key XOR, **not** the inverse-S-box read this project has been describing. (The S-box reads are
  at `0x792c59` and nearby.)
- `.pdata` says the enclosing function is **`[0x792b1c, 0x792ec3)`**.
- There are **no `cc cc cc` runs at all in `[0x792000, 0x792c78)`**. The nearest one is at `0x791f8d`,
  which is the entry of `AES_set_encrypt_key` — a *different* function. The recipe would have returned
  that one.

**The reliable way is `.pdata`, and the DLL has it.** `PlayerLibRender56_vs.dll` is not packed: six
normal sections, `.pdata` at RVA `0x12a8000` with **19,488** function entries, each `(start, end,
unwind)`. A function's entry is a lookup, not a scan. The same is true of `.text` in general — this
DLL is fully statically analysable from the file.

**And the disassembler this project believed it did not have is installed.** `capstone 5.0.7` and
`pefile 2024.8.26` are both present in `C:\Users\Yonjay\.conda\envs\subgen`. The old note "静态分析不可用：
无 capstone/pefile/dumpbin" is wrong — most likely it was run against the PATH `python`, which is the
Microsoft Store placeholder and has neither. Two scripts were deleted by ticket 03 on that false
premise; see the correction recorded there.

One practical note for anyone writing a disassembly loop: `capstone.Cs.disasm` **stops at the first
undecodable byte** and silently returns a short iteration. Over this DLL it yielded 448 `call`
instructions instead of tens of thousands until `md.skipdata = True` was set. A scan that "found
nothing" is more likely to have stopped early than to have proved an absence.

## Why this ticket matters more than its size suggests

This is one of the two routes to the thing the project actually wants. If the player's AES can be
called, then `POST /student/getPlayTimeKeySignEVS*` can be replayed from outside for any lesson in the
catalogue, and the segment manifests can be pulled without a human opening anything. That is the
"no play-this-one-fetch-this-one" goal, minus the per-lesson playback that blocks it today.

## The oracle's entry points, located statically

Found by disassembling the DLL from the file — no player needed for this part. All RVAs, image base
`0x180000000`.

**`0x20EC0` — the app's AES key setup.** `(rcx = the AES_KEY to fill, rdx = ?, r8d = bits, r9d = mode)`.
It selects a block function by mode and stores it, then expands the key:

```
0x020ef0  mov   rdi, rcx
0x020ef3  mov   [rsp+0x28], r9d        ; mode
0x020ef8  mov   ebx, r8d               ; bits
0x020f00  sar   ebx, 5                 ; nk = bits / 32
0x020f03  lea   rax, [rip-0x63a]       ; encrypt block function
0x020f12  lea   rcx, [rip-0xbd9]       ; decrypt block function
0x020f1c  cmovne rax, rcx              ; mode != 0 -> decrypt
0x020f27  mov   [rdi+0x118], rax       ; the chosen block function
0x020f2e  lea   r12d, [rbx+6]          ; rounds = nk + 6
```

The loop that follows (`0x11b`, a `0..0xff` byte table) is the GF(2^8) inverse table — a
constant-time AES, not OpenSSL's T-table version.

**`0x20EA0` — the block-call trampoline.** Call it with `rcx = ctx`:

```
0x020ea0  mov   eax, [rcx+0x110]       ; the round count
0x020ea6  mov   [rsp+0x30], eax
0x020eaa  jmp   qword [rcx+0x118]      ; tail-call the block function
```

So the minimum oracle is two calls and one allocation: allocate ~0x200 bytes for the AES_KEY, call
`0x20EC0` with the key you want to use (mode 0 to encrypt, nonzero to decrypt), then call `0x20EA0`
with that buffer. Nothing has to be recovered from the process, and nothing is hard-coded to one
captured message — which is what the acceptance criteria ask for.

**`AES_set_encrypt_key` at `0x791F90` and `AES_set_decrypt_key` at `0x791D10`** are the OpenSSL T-table
versions, called from 8 and 4 functions respectively, and they are on the *segment* path rather than
this one. `AES_set_encrypt_key` even appears among its own callers, which is the OpenSSL structure
(the decrypt-key routine calls the encrypt-key one).

**`0x3F4C0` — the second consumer of a context's key field.**

```
0x3f4c0  sub   rsp, 0x38
0x3f4c4  cmp   byte [rcx+0x264], 0      ; the ready byte
0x3f4cb  je    +0x1d
0x3f4cd  add   rcx, 0x120               ; the key field
0x3f4d4  mov   dword [rsp+0x28], 1      ; mode = decrypt
0x3f4dc  mov   dword [rsp+0x20], 0
0x3f4dd  call  0x20E98                  ; -> the trampoline above
```

Called from `0x392A4`. With `hls_decode`, that makes **two and only two** places in the whole `.text`
that use `add rcx,0x120` — the segment-key field has exactly two consumers, and both pass it to the
app's AES. That is worth knowing for ticket 09: the field really is an AES key, and the AES is this one.

**A note on what `+0x120` is.** `hls_decode` passes `ctx+0x120` as the *first* argument to the key
setup, i.e. as the AES_KEY to be filled in place. So the 32 bytes this project has been calling "the
schedule" are the head of an expanded key schedule, which is consistent with the empirical relation
`schedule_to_key` inverts — but it means the field is written **by the AES setup**, expanded from a
key handed to it. Whatever produces that input key is ticket 07's writer, and it is one call away
rather than in the same instruction.

# 03 — Classify the research bench and delete what the product already covers

**What to build:** Every script under the research bench gets exactly one verdict — the Rust product already covers it, it is still an instrument, or it cannot work against this build — and the covered and dead ones are deleted rather than described. Instruments are left alone: they are the apparatus tickets 06–10 run on, and rewriting them mid-experiment is the thing to avoid.

**Blocked by:** None — can start immediately

**Status:** ready-for-agent

- [x] Every script has a recorded verdict with a one-line reason.
- [x] Scripts whose capability the Rust product already implements are deleted.
- [x] Scripts that cannot work against this build are deleted.
- [x] Instruments survive untouched, and the list of them is what tickets 06–10 draw from.
- [x] Nothing the product or the remaining experiments depend on is deleted.

## Verdicts

31 Python scripts and one PowerShell script, each with one verdict. Twenty-one files were deleted in
all: eighteen Python scripts, the PowerShell script, and two `.cmd` wrappers. Thirteen Python scripts
survive as instruments.

### Covered by the product — deleted

The capability is now implemented in Rust, and the Rust version is the one that is correct. Every
harvest-family script here tests candidates against segment bytes; the bench's versions all predate
the 752-byte probe alignment fix, so their "0 hits" readings were artefacts of the bug.

| Script | Why it goes |
| --- | --- |
| `scan_ctypes.py` | ReadProcessMemory-only key scan — its own docstring names `evmedia-win/scan.rs` as the target, and that is now what the product does. |
| `fast_scan.py` | Scans memory for 32-hex candidates and tests them against the recently-written segments; that candidate path is `keyscan::recover`. |
| `harvest_all.py` | Memory scan, test against every downloaded segment, write JSON — the same job as `grab` plus `keyscan::recover`. |
| `harvest_keys.py` | Collects every 32-hex string and tries each as a key — superseded by the same path. |
| `scan_keys_all.py` | `harvest_keys.py` with a better target set; superseded the same way. |
| `try_keys.py` | Tests captured keys against real ciphertext — that test is `keyscan::recover`. |
| `ev2_grab.py` | The entire Python pipeline, harvest through merge; the Rust `grab` does all of it, including resume. |
| `drive_playhead.py` | Posts arrow keys to steer the playhead; `evmedia-win::playhead` does this, and its docstring says so. |

### Cannot work against this build — deleted

| Script | Why it goes |
| --- | --- |
| `ev2_batch.py` | Derives keys from manifests with the documented salt formula. That formula does not hold in this build, so without a salt it has no route to a key. |
| `hunt_salt.py` | Searches for the `tk + filename + salt` concatenation in memory. The decisive negative is that this build never builds that string. |
| `compare_tk.py` | Exists only to feed the tk-derivation family, which is the same disproven formula. |
| `find_b64.py` | Locates the base64 decoder by watching alphabet tables; repeated full-memory runs found nothing, and ticket 06 no longer needs the decoder. |
| `aes_map.py` | Static function-boundary mapping of the AES region — needs a disassembler the bench does not have, and the entry points it sought (`0x791F90`, `0x792c78`) are already known. |
| `aes_disasm.py` | Same static route to the same already-known RVA. |
| `disas.py` | Same static route again, against a live module; it times out. |
| `walk_aes.py` | Hooks the AES T-table site and walks up to its caller. The callers live in heap-generated code, so the walk reaches nothing — that is the finding, not a bug in the script. |
| `hexdiff.py` | The differential scan is broken (returns in 0.1 s with zero rows, i.e. it never scanned), and its question is now asked directly by ticket 07's write breakpoint, which needs no diff. |
| `_extract.py` | A one-off that pulled text out of a single, long-superseded session transcript into a log. It is not apparatus for anything pending. |
| `find_segments.ps1` | Its RVAs point at this build's M3U8 parser, not at key derivation. It has failed every time it was run. |

### Wrappers on the dead offline path — deleted

- `一键抓取.cmd` — exists only to run `find_segments.ps1`.
- `解密转MP4.cmd` — consumes the `evplayer2_manifest.json` that `find_segments.ps1` would have produced, so it cannot run either.

The vendored third-party directories and the two `.zip` archives (`EVPlayer2_解密工具与参数/`,
`EVPlayer2通用解密工具/`, and both zips) are **left in place**. They are not bench scripts, they are
tracked, and the zips are the authoritative copy of the vendor material. They sit on the same dead
offline path as the two wrappers above — worth knowing, but removing someone else's artefact is not
this ticket.

### Instruments — kept untouched

These are what tickets 06–10 draw from. `probe_urls.py` and `capture_all.py` overlap (the latter is
the v6 successor to the former); both are kept, because pruning apparatus mid-experiment is the thing
this ticket exists to avoid.

- **Ticket 06 (the API AES as an oracle):** `probe_at.py`, `hook_aes_key.py`, `find_aes_key.py`, `extract_bodies.py`.
- **Ticket 07 (the instruction that writes a segment key):** `probe_at.py`, `probe_schedule_key.py`, `wait_ready.py`, and `watch_key.py` — the last of which cannot be run as it stands. **Added after this classification, not part of the thirteen:** `tools/parser-tools/probe_write.py`, written when ticket 07 was made ready to run. `watch_key.py` is the only survivor that can arm a memory write watch and it is the one that hangs the player, so waiting on it would have cost the session the ticket exists for. Ticket 07 records what replaced it and why.
- **Ticket 08 (the `getDownEVSKey` plaintext):** `capture_all.py`, `sniff_plain.py`, `fish_api_plain.py`, `probe_urls.py`.
- **Both / general:** `hook_caller.py`, `find_in_mem.py`.

The count is therefore fourteen Python scripts on the bench today, not the thirteen this ticket left. The fourteenth arrived with ticket 07's preparation, after the classification was made.

### Dependency check

Nothing the product or the remaining experiments need was deleted. A repo-wide search for each
deleted name found only: `HANDOFF.md` (historical narrative, handled in ticket 05), `captured/harvest_all.log`
(capture evidence, which stays), and `scan_keys_all.py` inside the harvest family, deleted with it.
`disas.py`'s only other match is `tools/device_analysis/disasm.py`, a different file in a different
directory, untouched.

# 03 — Classify the research bench and delete what the product already covers

**What to build:** Every script under the research bench gets exactly one verdict — the Rust product already covers it, it is still an instrument, or it cannot work against this build — and the covered and dead ones are deleted rather than described. Instruments are left alone: they are the apparatus tickets 06–10 run on, and rewriting them mid-experiment is the thing to avoid.

**Blocked by:** None — can start immediately

**Status:** ready-for-agent

- [x] Every script has a recorded verdict with a one-line reason.
- [x] Scripts whose capability the Rust product already implements are deleted.
- [x] Scripts that cannot work against this build are deleted.
- [x] Instruments survive untouched, and the list of them is what tickets 06–10 draw from.
- [x] Nothing the product or the remaining experiments depend on is deleted.

## Verdicts

31 Python scripts and one PowerShell script, each with one verdict. Twenty-one files were deleted in
all: eighteen Python scripts, the PowerShell script, and two `.cmd` wrappers. Thirteen Python scripts
survive as instruments.

### Covered by the product — deleted

The capability is now implemented in Rust, and the Rust version is the one that is correct. Every
harvest-family script here tests candidates against segment bytes; the bench's versions all predate
the 752-byte probe alignment fix, so their "0 hits" readings were artefacts of the bug.

| Script | Why it goes |
| --- | --- |
| `scan_ctypes.py` | ReadProcessMemory-only key scan — its own docstring names `evmedia-win/scan.rs` as the target, and that is now what the product does. |
| `fast_scan.py` | Scans memory for 32-hex candidates and tests them against the recently-written segments; that candidate path is `keyscan::recover`. |
| `harvest_all.py` | Memory scan, test against every downloaded segment, write JSON — the same job as `grab` plus `keyscan::recover`. |
| `harvest_keys.py` | Collects every 32-hex string and tries each as a key — superseded by the same path. |
| `scan_keys_all.py` | `harvest_keys.py` with a better target set; superseded the same way. |
| `try_keys.py` | Tests captured keys against real ciphertext — that test is `keyscan::recover`. |
| `ev2_grab.py` | The entire Python pipeline, harvest through merge; the Rust `grab` does all of it, including resume. |
| `drive_playhead.py` | Posts arrow keys to steer the playhead; `evmedia-win::playhead` does this, and its docstring says so. |

### Cannot work against this build — deleted

| Script | Why it goes |
| --- | --- |
| `ev2_batch.py` | Derives keys from manifests with the documented salt formula. That formula does not hold in this build, so without a salt it has no route to a key. |
| `hunt_salt.py` | Searches for the `tk + filename + salt` concatenation in memory. The decisive negative is that this build never builds that string. |
| `compare_tk.py` | Exists only to feed the tk-derivation family, which is the same disproven formula. |
| `find_b64.py` | Locates the base64 decoder by watching alphabet tables; repeated full-memory runs found nothing, and ticket 06 no longer needs the decoder. |
| `aes_map.py` | Static function-boundary mapping of the AES region. **Deleted on a false premise — see the correction below.** |
| `aes_disasm.py` | Same static route to the same RVA. **Deleted on a false premise — see the correction below.** |
| `disas.py` | Same static route again, against a live module; it times out. |
| `walk_aes.py` | Hooks the AES T-table site and walks up to its caller. The callers live in heap-generated code, so the walk reaches nothing — that is the finding, not a bug in the script. |
| `hexdiff.py` | The differential scan is broken (returns in 0.1 s with zero rows, i.e. it never scanned), and its question is now asked directly by ticket 07's write breakpoint, which needs no diff. |
| `_extract.py` | A one-off that pulled text out of a single, long-superseded session transcript into a log. It is not apparatus for anything pending. |
| `find_segments.ps1` | Its RVAs point at this build's M3U8 parser, not at key derivation. It has failed every time it was run. |

### Wrappers on the dead offline path — deleted

- `一键抓取.cmd` — exists only to run `find_segments.ps1`.
- `解密转MP4.cmd` — consumes the `evplayer2_manifest.json` that `find_segments.ps1` would have produced, so it cannot run either.

The vendored third-party directories and the two `.zip` archives (`EVPlayer2_解密工具与参数/`,
`EVPlayer2通用解密工具/`, and both zips) are **left in place**. They are not bench scripts, they are
tracked, and the zips are the authoritative copy of the vendor material. They sit on the same dead
offline path as the two wrappers above — worth knowing, but removing someone else's artefact is not
this ticket.

### Instruments — kept untouched

These are what tickets 06–10 draw from. `probe_urls.py` and `capture_all.py` overlap (the latter is
the v6 successor to the former); both are kept, because pruning apparatus mid-experiment is the thing
this ticket exists to avoid.

- **Ticket 06 (the API AES as an oracle):** `probe_at.py`, `hook_aes_key.py`, `find_aes_key.py`, `extract_bodies.py`.
- **Ticket 07 (the instruction that writes a segment key):** `probe_at.py`, `probe_schedule_key.py`, `wait_ready.py`, and `watch_key.py` — the last of which cannot be run as it stands. **Added after this classification, not part of the thirteen:** `tools/parser-tools/probe_write.py`, written when ticket 07 was made ready to run. `watch_key.py` is the only survivor that can arm a memory write watch and it is the one that hangs the player, so waiting on it would have cost the session the ticket exists for. Ticket 07 records what replaced it and why.
- **Ticket 08 (the `getDownEVSKey` plaintext):** `capture_all.py`, `sniff_plain.py`, `fish_api_plain.py`, `probe_urls.py`.
- **Both / general:** `hook_caller.py`, `find_in_mem.py`.

The count is therefore fourteen Python scripts on the bench today, not the thirteen this ticket left. The fourteenth arrived with ticket 07's preparation, after the classification was made.

### Dependency check

Nothing the product or the remaining experiments need was deleted. A repo-wide search for each
deleted name found only: `HANDOFF.md` (historical narrative, handled in ticket 05), `captured/harvest_all.log`
(capture evidence, which stays), and `scan_keys_all.py` inside the harvest family, deleted with it.
`disas.py`'s only other match is `tools/device_analysis/disasm.py`, a different file in a different
directory, untouched.

```
six reads of the guarded page, then a 32-byte store -- survived the reads, caught the
```
